edges.description: Selected NR5A1 missense variants reduce a steroidogenic-promoter reporter in transfected cells; this does not establish the effect of every allele.
The genetic association establishes a developmental effect, but the causal fetal targets and thresholds vary and are not resolved for each allele.
Patient-derived and transfected-cell assays identify increased association for selected variants.
The p.Arg186Gly construct shows reduced ubiquitination in HEK293T cells; mediation by increased RHOA binding remains an interpretation.
The p.Arg186Gly construct produces more MAP3K1 protein in NT2/D1 and KGN cells.
Selected patient lymphoblastoid lines show altered ERK phosphorylation after serum refeeding.
The response occurs in selected patient lines and p.Arg186Gly overexpression models, with allele-dependent differences.
The p.Arg186Gly construct increases TCF/LEF reporter activity; intervening signaling was not dissected by epistasis.
Human pedigrees and cases support MAP3K1-related partial dysgenesis. The observed signaling changes propose, but do not experimentally reconstruct, the human fetal developmental route.
Human biallelic DHH cases include histologically confirmed partial dysgenesis.
Loss of mature Leydig-cell staining in one partial gonad supports a developmental differentiation abnormality; the intervening paracrine mechanism remains inferred.
The original molecularly characterized patient had minifascicular nerve pathology; the intermediate human developmental signaling was not measured.
Overexpression experiments found lower protein abundance for p.Arg308Gln and selected other variants. The effect is assay-specific and does not prove reduced helicase activity.
The p.Arg308Gln patient had biopsy-documented bilateral dysgenetic testes. Intermediates between the variant and fetal gonadal development remain unknown.
The whole-gene deletion case directly documents severe partial dysgenesis; the disrupted fetal transcriptional program was not assayed.
Pathogenic WT1 variants predispose to glomerular disease within WT1 disorder. This is restricted to the WT1-related subtype; intervening renal cellular mechanisms are not modeled here.

Wilms tumor occurred in the child with a WT1 whole-gene deletion and partial gonadal dysgenesis. This genotype-qualified link does not imply that every variant or affected person develops a tumor, or that the somatic initiating events were measured.
Histology is a direct readout of abnormal tissue differentiation.
Müllerian retention in a subset is consistent with insufficient fetal AMH action; this is a developmental inference, not a fetal serum measurement.
Undervirilized external genital development is consistent with inadequate fetal testicular androgen activity; timing and output are inferred rather than measured.
Abnormal tubular and germ-cell architecture plausibly contributes to the semen abnormalities observed in clinical follow-up; patient-specific mediation is not experimentally demonstrated.
OCT3/4-positive luminal cells in a MAP3K1-associated partial gonad demonstrate delayed maturation within dysgenetic tissue.
Underdeveloped testicular tissue is consistent with reduced volume in the reported NR5A1 case. The contribution of each histological compartment was not quantified.

Primary gonadal dysfunction can reduce sex-steroid output and feedback, producing elevated gonadotropins with low testosterone in a subset; preserved androgen production in other partial cases remains compatible with dysgenesis.
Insufficient fetal AMH action permits Müllerian structures to persist; regression failure is the omitted developmental intermediate.
Incomplete androgen-dependent external genital differentiation is the physiological interpretation of the partial phenotype.
Incomplete androgen-dependent urethral development is an inferred developmental explanation for this observed feature.
Insufficient androgen-dependent phallic growth provides the developmental interpretation of reduced phallic size.
Severe failure of sperm production can result in an azoospermic ejaculate; observed in individual cases, not all PGD.
Impaired sperm production can limit fertility; individual reproductive potential is not determined by androgen production alone.
Reduced sperm production is reflected by the severe oligozoospermia observed in the three semen-tested participants.

nodes.description: Discuss gonadal function, genotype, tissue location, available pathology, age, fertility potential and the individual's goals with an experienced DSD team. Nonfunctional high-risk dysgenetic gonads may warrant removal; potentially functional gonads may be retained after individualized discussion. Sex assignment and a preserved hCG response are not stand-alone indications for removal or retention. Surveillance options exist, but no strategy reliably excludes neoplasia; the registry percentages are selected histology prevalences rather than prospective risks for retained gonads.

nodes.description: Replace sex steroids when gonadal production is insufficient or after gonadectomy, according to the individual's desired pubertal development and clinical needs. Testosterone or 17-beta-estradiol is introduced gradually with monitoring; an endometrium-bearing uterus requires addition of progestogen after appropriate estrogen priming. Spontaneous pubertal onset does not guarantee completion. Endo-ERN guidance supports individualized induction around age 11 for girls with confirmed hypogonadism and around age 12 for boys at high risk without pubertal onset. These recommendations cover broader congenital hypogonadism; the guideline found no eligible comparative puberty-treatment studies specifically in males with PGD.
